# Trends {#sec-trends}

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

<!-- Trendline material adapted from DSCI 531 lecture 5,
     originally introduced in the communication chapter. -->

:::: {.slide-outcomes}

::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. **Use** means and rolling means to summarize patterns while retaining the observations as context.
2. **Distinguish** global regression models from local smoothing, and **choose** a trendline according to the question and audience.
3. **Adjust** smoothing neighborhoods and **explain** how they affect the local detail shown by a curve.
4. **Recognize** that describing a trend within the observed data does not justify extrapolating it beyond that range.

:::

::::

```{python}
#| label: trends-python-setup
#| include: false
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

cars = pd.read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv').dropna(subset=['Acceleration', 'Horsepower'])
```

```{r}
#| label: trends-r-setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_gray(base_size = 14))
cars <- read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv', show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    drop_na(Acceleration, Horsepower)
```

## Why bother?

In @sec-connections, lines connected observations to show relationships and changes.
Here we use lines to summarize a pattern rather than connect every observation.
[A trendline can make a general pattern easier to see when individual observations
or multiple groups obscure it.]{.slide-bullet}
Trendlines are also called fitted lines or lines of best fit.
The choice of line determines which features of the data are emphasized.
Here we focus on the summaries themselves and keep the observations visible.
In @sec-uncertainty, we add intervals and distinguish the spread of observations
from uncertainty in an estimated mean.

We use automobile specifications from the Vega datasets collection,
with missing acceleration or horsepower observations omitted.
`Acceleration` records the time in seconds to accelerate from 0 to 60 mph:
a larger value means the car takes longer to reach that speed.
We first examine how horsepower varies with acceleration time across all cars,
using one trendline. Near the end of the chapter, we compare this pooled relationship
with separate fits by origin.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-car-points-alt
#| slide-show: both
points = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle(opacity=0.2).encode(
    x=alt.X('Acceleration:Q').scale(zero=False),
    y='Horsepower'
)
points
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-car-points-gg
#| slide-show: both
car_points <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Acceleration, y = Horsepower)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2)
car_points
```

:::

## Why bother? {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

[Connecting every observation without any aggregation does not provide a useful summary of the trend]{.slide-bullet}.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-connected-points-alt
#| slide-show: both
points + points.mark_line()
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-connected-points-gg
#| slide-show: both
car_points + geom_line()
```

:::

::::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

The four panels below show the same cars on the same axis scales,
but summarize the relationship in different ways.
Before learning how to construct the lines, consider what each might be estimating.

:::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-opening-comparison-alt
#| echo: false
#| slide-show: output
comparison_points = points.mark_circle(opacity=0.3)
comparison_mean = alt.Chart(cars).mark_rule(color='#4C78A8', size=2).encode(y='mean(Horsepower):Q')
comparison_linear = points.mark_line().transform_regression('Acceleration', 'Horsepower')
comparison_rolling = points.mark_line().transform_window(
    rolling_hp='mean(Horsepower)', frame=[-30, 30],
    sort=[alt.SortField('Acceleration')]
).encode(y='rolling_hp:Q')
comparison_local = points.mark_line().transform_loess(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower', bandwidth=0.5
)
trend_comparison_alt = alt.vconcat(
    alt.hconcat(
        (comparison_points + comparison_mean).properties(width=250, height=170, title='A'),
        (comparison_points + comparison_linear).properties(width=250, height=170, title='B')
    ).resolve_scale(x='shared', y='shared'),
    alt.hconcat(
        (comparison_points + comparison_rolling).properties(width=250, height=170, title='C'),
        (comparison_points + comparison_local).properties(width=250, height=170, title='D')
    ).resolve_scale(x='shared', y='shared')
).resolve_scale(x='shared', y='shared')
trend_comparison_alt
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-opening-comparison-gg
#| echo: false
#| slide-show: output
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
comparison_points <- ggplot(cars, aes(x = Acceleration, y = Horsepower)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = range(cars$Acceleration), ylim = c(0, max(cars$Horsepower)))
comparison_rolling_cars <- cars |>
    arrange(Acceleration) |>
    mutate(rolling_hp = slider::slide_dbl(
        Horsepower, mean, .before = 30, .after = 30
    ))
comparison_mean <- comparison_points +
    geom_hline(yintercept = mean(cars$Horsepower), color = '#3366FF') + labs(title = 'A')
comparison_linear <- comparison_points +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE) + labs(title = 'B')
comparison_rolling <- comparison_points +
    geom_line(data = comparison_rolling_cars, color = '#3366FF', aes(y = rolling_hp)) + labs(title = 'C')
comparison_local <- comparison_points +
    geom_smooth(method = 'loess', span = 0.5, se = FALSE,
                method.args = list(degree = 1, family = 'symmetric')) + labs(title = 'D')
trend_comparison_gg <- patchwork::wrap_plots(
    comparison_mean, comparison_linear, comparison_rolling, comparison_local, ncol = 2
) & theme(text = element_text(size = 11))
trend_comparison_gg
```

::::

:::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

[Think about whether the prediction is constant, changes at a constant rate,
or changes its behavior across the x-axis.]{.slide-bullet}

::::

Keep your proposed explanations in mind as you work through the chapter.
We will revisit the same figure and identify the four methods in @sec-trend-summary-comparison.

:::::

### Averaging at each exact value

[A simple summary is the mean horsepower at each acceleration time.]{.slide-bullet}
[Some acceleration times occur repeatedly, but others have very few observations,]{.slide-bullet}
resulting in [a noisy appearance of the line with many spikes
that makes it hard to see the overall trend]{.slide-subbullet}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-exact-mean-alt
#| slide-show: both
points + points.mark_line().encode(y='mean(Horsepower)')
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-exact-mean-gg
#| slide-show: both
car_points + geom_line(stat = 'summary', fun = 'mean')
```

:::

Each mean is calculated separately from the observations at that acceleration time.
Connecting the estimates helps us follow the pattern, but does not change the estimates
or fit a shared model across the x-range.

### Binned means

For a continuous x variable, we could instead [divide its range into bins
and calculate the mean response within each bin]{.slide-bullet}.
A histogram uses these intervals to count observations;
here we use them to average a response variable.
The example below uses three-second acceleration intervals.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-binned-mean-alt
#| slide-show: both
points + points.mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('Acceleration:Q').bin(step=3),
    y='mean(Horsepower)'
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

We use `stat = 'summary_bin'` to allow us to define a custom summary
function with the bin instead of counting the observations.

```{r}
#| label: trends-binned-mean-gg
#| slide-show: both
car_points + geom_line(stat = 'summary_bin', fun = mean, binwidth = 3)
```

:::

Binned means give a first view of the pattern, but depend on the width and placement
of the bins. Bins can contain very different numbers of cars,
and a single mean hides any pattern within its interval.
Connecting these summaries adds interpolation between them, not a fitted model for the whole dataset.

We will now explore two ways to estimate the pattern more systematically:
fit one model across the full range, or fit simple models within moving neighborhoods.

## Fitting a global model

Another way to summarize the data is to [fit one shared equation across the observed range]{.slide-bullet}.
Here, a **model** is a rule that uses an input value to produce a predicted response.
[The simplest model returns the same prediction for every input]{.slide-bullet}.
[We will build up the flexibility of that equation in three steps]{.slide-bullet}:

::: {.slide-bullet}

- **One mean for all observations:** give every car the same predicted horsepower.
- **Allow the line to tilt:** let the prediction change with acceleration time.
- **Allow the relationship to curve:** add a squared acceleration feature.

:::

We use least-squares fitting throughout this progression.
[Unlike separate means at each acceleration time,
a regression links estimates across
acceleration times through shared coefficients]{.slide-bullet}.
Changing observations in one part of the x-range can change fitted values throughout the range.
This pooling can stabilize estimates, but it can also hide abrupt changes
or impose an unsuitable shape; a shared model is not automatically better.

### One mean for all observations

If we had to predict every car's horsepower using the same value,
which value would minimize the sum of squared errors?
Unlike the earlier means at individual acceleration times or within bins,
this estimate uses all cars to make one prediction shared by every observation.

[The mean is the constant that minimizes the sum of squared deviations]{.slide-bullet}.
In graphical terms, it is [the best-fitting horizontal line under squared-error loss]{.slide-subbullet}.
Here $i$ indexes cars, $\hat{y}_i$ is predicted horsepower, and $w_0$ is the fitted constant:

::: {.slide-text}

$$
\hat{y}_i = w_0 = \bar{y}
$$

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-global-mean-alt
#| slide-show: both
global_mean = alt.Chart(cars).mark_rule().encode(y='mean(Horsepower):Q')
points + global_mean
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-global-mean-gg
#| slide-show: both
car_points + geom_hline(yintercept = mean(cars$Horsepower))
```

:::

### Allow the model to tilt

Can we improve the predictions by allowing them to depend on acceleration time?
[Linear least-squares regression fits a straight line by minimizing the sum
of squared vertical deviations from the observations to the line.]{.slide-bullet}
[Linear regression allows that line to tilt by estimating a slope in addition to the intercept]{.slide-bullet}.
The horizontal mean line is a special case where the slope is constrained to zero.
For the straight-line fit, we estimate

::: {.slide-text}

$$
\hat{y}_i = w_0 + x_{i1}w_1
$$

:::

[where $i$ indexes cars, $x_{i1}$ is car $i$'s acceleration time in seconds,
and $\hat{y}_i$ is its predicted mean horsepower.]{.slide-bullet}
The fitted weights $w_0$ and $w_1$ are the intercept and slope.
The first subscript in $x_{i1}$ identifies the observation; the second identifies the feature.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-linear-fit-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: A linear trend
points + points.mark_line().transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower'
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

Set the smoothing method to `lm` for a linear model.
`se = FALSE` hides ggplot's default confidence band,
which we will instead talk about in @sec-uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: trends-linear-fit-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: A linear trend
car_points + geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE)
```

:::

### Allow the model to curve

What if one constant slope does not capture the pattern?
Regression is not restricted to straight lines.
[For the degree-two polynomial below, we add a feature $x_{i2} = x_{i1}^2$:]{.slide-bullet}

::: {.slide-text}

$$
\hat{y}_i = w_0 + x_{i1}w_1 + x_{i2}w_2
$$

:::

The weight $w_2$ on squared acceleration time allows the relationship to curve
rather than have a constant slope.
All three examples estimate their coefficients using all cars by minimizing
the sum of squared vertical residuals.
[The quadratic fit is still a linear model in its weights $w_0$, $w_1$, and $w_2$,
even though its graph can be curved in the original feature space.]{.slide-bullet}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}


```{python}
#| label: trends-polynomial-fit-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: A polynomial trend
points + points.mark_line().transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower', method='poly', order=2
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-polynomial-fit-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: A polynomial trend
car_points +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm', formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), se = FALSE)
```

:::

## Fitting local models

Sometimes one equation is a poor description of the whole dataset.
[Instead of fitting one model across the full range, we can fit simple models
repeatedly to nearby observations.]{.slide-bullet}
We will follow the same progression as before:
start with a constant, then allow each local fit to tilt.

[Binning uses fixed, non-overlapping neighborhoods.]{.slide-bullet}
[A rolling mean instead averages observations within overlapping neighborhoods
that move along the axis.]{.slide-bullet}
[We can think of a rolling mean as **local constant regression**:
at each target x-value, fit a horizontal line to nearby observations
and retain its height as the estimate.]{.slide-bullet}
The resulting curve can bend even though each individual fit is horizontal,
because the observations contributing to the estimate change as the neighborhood moves.

Here we sort the individual cars by acceleration time and average neighboring
observations across all origins. Each included car receives equal weight.
Unlike fixed bins, the neighborhoods overlap;
however, equal-weight windows can still produce jumps as observations enter or leave.

:::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

`frame=[-30, 30]` starts with the preceding 30 observations, the current observation,
and the following 30 observations in acceleration-time order.
At the endpoints, it uses the available observations.
By default, Altair expands window boundaries to include ties in the sorting variable,
so a window can include more than 61 cars when acceleration times repeat.

```{python}
#| label: trends-rolling-window-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Rolling means as local constant fits
alt.Chart(cars).transform_window(
    rolling_hp='mean(Horsepower)',
    frame=[-30, 30],
    sort=[alt.SortField('Acceleration')]
).mark_line().encode(
    x=alt.X('Acceleration:Q'),
    y='rolling_hp:Q'
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

There is no built-in way to plot a rolling mean in ggplot,
so instead we calculate the means before plotting.
`slider::slide_dbl()` averages the preceding 30 rows, the current row, and the following
30 rows, using the available rows at the endpoints.
Unlike Altair's default, this uses strict row boundaries rather than expanding for ties,
so the curves can differ where acceleration times repeat.

```{r}
#| label: trends-rolling-window-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Rolling means as local constant fits
rolling_cars <- cars |>
    arrange(Acceleration) |>
    mutate(rolling_hp = slider::slide_dbl(
        Horsepower, mean, .before = 30, .after = 30
    ))
ggplot(rolling_cars, aes(x = Acceleration, y = rolling_hp)) +
    geom_line()
```

::::

### Choosing a rolling window

The width of 30 observations on either side is an illustrative starting point,
not a generally optimal choice. Compare narrower and wider windows to see which
features persist. A fixed observation count spans different ranges of acceleration times
where cars are more or less densely represented.
Repeated acceleration times can also receive different estimates as the row window moves,
producing vertical segments when those estimates are connected at the same x-value.

Three window types answer different questions:

::: {.slide-bullet}

- **Expanding** (`[None, 0]`, the default in Altair): average everything up to the current position in the sort order.
  This estimates a cumulative level rather than a local trend.
- **Trailing** (for example, `[-30, 0]`): use observations at or before the current position. Common in e.g. finance.
  With a chronological sort, this is useful for monitoring as observations arrive.
- **Centered** (`[-30, 30]`): use observations on both sides to describe a local pattern. Common in e.g. statistics.

:::

### Allow each local fit to tilt

[Local linear regression instead fits a line with a slope,
then evaluates that line at the target x-value.]{.slide-bullet}
Moving the neighborhood and repeating these fits produces the curve.
LOESS (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing), also called LOWESS
(locally weighted scatterplot smoothing), uses local fits with distance-based weights.
Nearby observations receive more influence, and the local fits can be linear or quadratic.
The animation builds up the red fitted curve from local fits.

::: {.slide-fragment}

![A local regression curve is assembled by moving a fitting window across the observations. Animation by Rafael Irizarry, from [Simply Statistics](https://simplystatistics.org/posts/2017-08-08-code-for-my-educational-gifs/).](img/loess-local-regression.gif)

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

Altair fits linear regression locally in each neighborhood in `transform_loess`.
<!-- TODO this should go in a deep dive -->
<!-- There is also residual-based robust fitting -->
<!-- that creates many fits iteratively -->
<!-- and reduces the influence of observations that lie unusually far from an initial fitted trend -->
<!-- maybe also talk about kernel weighting -->

```{python}
#| label: trends-loess-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: A local trend
points + points.mark_line().transform_loess(
    'Acceleration',
    'Horsepower',
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}

For computational efficiency,
`geom_smooth()` automatically changes the method based on the number of data points.
To ensure that we use LOESS,
we therefore set it explicitly although it is the default for datasets
up to 1000 observations per group.
By default,
ggplot fits quadratic regressions locally for each neighborhood.

```{r}
#| label: trends-loess-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: A local trend
car_points + geom_smooth(method = 'loess', se = FALSE)
```

:::

::: {.deep-dive}

### Choosing the smoothing neighborhood size

| Setting | Altair | ggplot |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Local fit | Linear | Quadratic |
| Neighborhood fraction | `bandwidth=0.3` | `span=0.75` |

The examples start with each library's defaults.
Changing the neighborhood fraction
does not by itself make the fits equivalent.

We can control the fraction of observations included in each neighborhood.
Larger fractions usually give a smoother, more general curve.
Note that even if we were to include all observations in each neighborhood,
this would not generally be identical to a single global linear regression
since all observations do not have the same weight.

:::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

#### Altair {.slide-skip}

The `bandwidth` parameter controls the fraction of observations included in each neighborhood.
By default,
it is set to 0.3.

```{python}
#| label: trends-loess-bandwidth-alt
points + points.mark_line().transform_loess(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower', bandwidth=0.75
)
```

#### ggplot {.slide-skip}


The `span` parameter changes the fraction of observations in each neighborhood.
By default,
it is set as 0.75.

```{r}
#| label: trends-loess-span-gg
car_points + geom_smooth(
    method = 'loess', span = 0.3, se = FALSE,
    method.args = list(degree = 1, family = 'symmetric')
)
```

::::

The following animations illustrate the qualitative effect of narrower and wider
weighting neighborhoods in a different LOWESS implementation.
Its Gaussian-width parameter, $\sigma$, is not the same parameter as Altair's bandwidth
or ggplot's span.

![A narrower weighting neighborhood follows more local variation. Source: [scikit-lego](https://scikit-lego.netlify.app/linear-models.html).](img/lowess-small-bandwidth.gif)

![A wider weighting neighborhood produces a smoother curve. Source: [scikit-lego](https://scikit-lego.netlify.app/linear-models.html).](img/lowess-large-bandwidth.gif)

:::

::: {.deep-dive}

### Kernels connect density estimation and local regression

In @sec-smoothed-distributions, kernels let observations contribute gradually
to nearby locations rather than placing them entirely inside one fixed bin.
[The same distance-based weighting idea can be used to estimate a relationship.]{.slide-bullet}

At a target x-value, a **rectangular kernel** gives equal weight to observations
inside a window and zero weight outside it.
A **Gaussian kernel** gives the greatest weight to nearby observations,
with smoothly decreasing weights at greater distances.
Its weights are technically nonzero everywhere.
The bandwidth controls the distance over which those weights decrease.

What we do with the weights determines what we estimate:

- **KDE:** add the kernel contributions and normalize to estimate the density of x.
- **Local weighted mean:** average the corresponding y-values, dividing by the sum of the weights.
- **Local linear regression:** use the weights to fit a nearby line, then evaluate it at the target.

With rectangular weights, the local weighted mean is a moving-window average.
With smoothly decreasing weights, it is often called a **kernel smoother**.
A KDE needs only the x-values; regression also needs a response variable y.
More observations near a location increase its estimated density,
but do not by themselves increase its estimated mean response.

LOESS commonly uses **tricube weights**, which decrease with distance
and reach zero at the edge of a nearest-neighbor neighborhood.
Its span specifies a fraction of observations,
whereas a KDE bandwidth commonly specifies a distance in the variable's units.
These settings therefore share an idea but are not directly interchangeable.
Likewise, a rolling window of 61 rows is not a fixed interval of acceleration times
when observations are unevenly spaced along the x-axis.

:::: {.callout-default .ex-prompt}

Suppose every car has exactly 100 horsepower, but many more cars have acceleration
times near 15 seconds than near 10 or 20 seconds.
Would a KDE of acceleration times and a local weighted mean of horsepower
both have a peak near 15 seconds?

::::: {.callout-default .ex-hint}

One calculation estimates where the x-values are concentrated;
the other averages the y-values associated with nearby x-values.

:::::: {.callout-default .ex-solution}

The KDE can have a peak where acceleration times are densely represented,
depending on its bandwidth.
The local weighted mean remains 100 wherever the total weight is positive:
its weighted sum is 100 times the sum of its weights,
so dividing by that sum returns 100.
The same kernels can therefore reveal a changing density and a constant response.

::::::
:::::
::::
:::

### Why fit a local slope? {.slide-skip}

Near the left edge of an increasing trend, most available neighbors lie to the right.
A rolling mean averages their higher responses and can overestimate the response at the target.
A local linear fit can account for the slope and evaluate the line at the target instead
For observations lying exactly on a straight line, it recovers that line wherever
the neighborhood contains enough distinct, positively weighted x-values.
A local mean can also reproduce a straight trend in a symmetric neighborhood,
but generally not at the boundaries or when the x-values are unevenly spaced.

In our examples, the rolling mean and regression both use individual cars as observations,
so densely represented acceleration ranges contribute more observations to their fits.
The rolling mean uses a centered observation window with equal weight per included car
(with boundary ties expanded in the Altair example);
LOESS instead selects a fraction of nearby cars and weights them by distance.
To isolate the effect of a local constant versus a local slope,
we would need to use the same input observations, neighborhoods, and weights.

## Compare the questions answered by different summaries {#sec-trend-summary-comparison}

Return to the opening exercise. The same four panels now illustrate a progression
from a global constant to a global line, and from a local constant to local regression.
The top row uses all cars to fit one shared model; the bottom row uses moving neighborhoods.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-comparison-alt
#| echo: false
#| slide-show: output
trend_comparison_alt
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-comparison-gg
#| echo: false
#| slide-show: output
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6
trend_comparison_gg
```

:::

Following more local variation is not automatically better:
the useful summary depends on the question and on which features persist
across reasonable modeling choices.

::: {.slide-visual slide-title="Comparing trend estimators"}

| Panel and summary | Observations used | What is fitted? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **A: Overall mean** | All cars | One shared constant |
| **B: Global linear regression** | All cars | One shared straight line |
| **C: Rolling mean** | Moving, overlapping window | A local constant |
| **D: Local smoothing regression (LOESS)** | Nearby cars, weighted by distance | A local line at each target |

:::

For this comparison, the rolling mean uses 30 observations on either side,
with the boundary-tie handling described earlier for each library.
Both LOESS examples use a neighborhood fraction of 0.5;
the R fit explicitly uses local linear, robust fitting to more closely match Altair.
The implementations can still give slightly different curves.

[Trend estimators differ in which observations they use, how they weight them,
and how flexible a function they fit.]{.slide-bullet}

## When to choose which trendline?

::: {.slide-bullet}

- **Means and rolling means** are useful when the summarized values should have
  a straightforward interpretation. It is poorly suited to extrapolation beyond the data range
  but can be particularly accessible to a general audience.
- **Regression models** are useful when a simple equation is a reasonable description
  of the relationship and it is advantageous to describe the relationship with a known equation.
  Predictions beyond the observed range
  are generally more accurate than for models fitted using a local neighborhood,
  but they still rely on that the fitted equation hold beyong the observed range,
  and become more uncertain as they move further from the data.
- **LOESS** is useful for describing patterns within the observed data without choosing
  one global equation. It often resembles the trend a reader would sketch by eye,
  and it generally usable for communication purposes although they are not as straightforward
  to understand as a rolling mean.
  It is poorly suited to extrapolation beyond the data range.

:::

## Extension: comparing trends within groups

So far, each trend has summarized all cars together.
[The pooled fit describes the overall relationship between acceleration time and horsepower.]{.slide-bullet}
[Separate fits by origin ask whether that relationship also describes the cars within each group.]{.slide-bullet}
As in @sec-groups, the overall pattern can reflect both differences within groups
and differences between groups.

In the following comparison, the colored lines are separate linear regressions
for each origin, and the dashed black line is the pooled regression from earlier.
Using the same fitting method lets us focus on the effect of grouping.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Altair {.slide-skip}

```{python}
#| label: trends-grouped-fit-alt
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Pooled and within-origin trends
grouped_points = points.encode(color='Origin:N')
grouped_lines = grouped_points.mark_line().transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower', groupby=['Origin']
)
pooled_line = points.mark_line(color='black', strokeDash=[6, 4]).transform_regression(
    'Acceleration', 'Horsepower'
)
grouped_points + grouped_lines + pooled_line
```

### ggplot {.slide-skip}

```{r}
#| label: trends-grouped-fit-gg
#| slide-show: both
#| slide-title: Pooled and within-origin trends
ggplot(cars, aes(x = Acceleration, y = Horsepower, color = Origin)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE) +
    geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), method = 'lm', se = FALSE,
                color = 'black', linetype = 'dashed')
```

:::

The pooled line need not coincide with any group's line.
Ask whether the groups occupy different parts of the x-range and whether their
slopes or fitted levels differ. The pooled and grouped fits answer different questions;
choose according to the comparison you want to make, rather than automatically
adding groups to every trend plot.
